An Afro-Futurist Commonwealth

We are not waiting
for the future.
We are building it.

Tomorrowland is a cooperative platform for community wealth, historical reclamation, and collective sovereignty — land, knowledge, and capital returned to the hands of the people who were promised them, and the children who are owed them still. We hold our treasury in common, our history in the open, and our future in no one's custody but our own.

The Pioneer Wall

Founders of the commons

Builders, elders, artists and engineers who committed the first hours, the first dollars, and the first dreams — back when Tomorrowland was a shared document, a standing Tuesday call, and a refusal to wait for permission that was never going to come.

“We did not inherit this earth from our ancestors. We are borrowing it from children who will ask us what we did with what was taken.”— Elder Maroon, opening of the first commons assembly

What makes a pioneer?

A pioneer is not an investor and not a customer. A pioneer is someone who shows up before there is anything to show up to — who contributes labor, capital, knowledge, or care while the outcome is still uncertain. Every name on this wall registered in the first ninety days, when Tomorrowland was a shared document and a standing Tuesday call.

Pioneers hold no special voting weight — the Signal is strictly one member, one voice. What they hold instead is memory: they were there, and the commons does not forget.

90

Days between the founding call and the first on-chain treasury proposal.

412

Volunteer hours logged by pioneers before the first dollar was ever deposited.

11

Time zones spanned by the founding circle — the commons has never slept.

Sovereign Registry

Sign your name on-chain

Register your Polygon wallet to join the commons. Your address becomes your membership credential — self-custodied, self-sovereign, revocable by no committee. There is no application and no approval queue; the wall accepts anyone willing to sign their name to the charter and stand behind it.

Your address is your credential. We never ask for seed phrases, and no real transaction is made in this demonstration.

From the Charter, Article One

“We, the members of the Tomorrowland Commons, hold these truths to be self-evident: that wealth pooled is wealth multiplied; that memory kept is territory held; that no institution will restore what it profited from erasing; and that we are therefore resolved to build, fund, teach, and remember — in common, on the record, and without apology.”

Ratified by the first Signal, 214 votes in favor, 3 against, 11 abstaining. The three dissenting votes are recorded with the same care as the rest — the commons keeps its disagreements too.

Collaboration Lanes

Choose your lane

Every contribution compounds — an hour of teaching becomes a credential, a dollar held long becomes an acre, a well-told story becomes a hundred new pioneers. Pick the lane that matches your gifts — or run in several; most members do.

How lanes interlock

Lanes are not departments; they are commitments of attention. A builder learns from the teach lane, the fund lane finances what builders ship, and the amplify lane makes sure the world — and the next generation of pioneers — hears about all of it. Members vote quarterly on lane budgets through the Signal, and every lane publishes an open ledger of hours and outcomes.

There is only one rule across all four: leave the commons stronger than you found it.

Tomorrowland Academy

The curriculum of liberation

Twenty-four essential texts and six guided study paths. Search the stacks, filter by discipline, download any primer as a text file. Everything here is free — the academy's only tuition is that you teach forward what you learn.

Study Guides

“A people that can read its own ledger, write its own contracts, and teach its own history is a people that cannot be erased twice.”— Dean Zuri Adebayo, Academy convocation address

How the Academy works

Every text in the canon is free. Every primer downloads as plain text — no accounts, no paywalls, no tracking. Study circles of six to twelve members meet for six-week seasons, guided by a facilitator from the teach lane. Completing a guide earns a credential recorded against your registry address: knowledge, like membership, is something you hold yourself.

Reclamation Ledger

Erased chapters, restored

Communities destroyed by violence, flood, and policy — remembered here with dignity, and honored through the work of rebuilding. Read each chapter slowly. These are not case studies; they are addresses. Some of them still have mail delivered to descendants who keep the key.

Rebuild Black Wall Street — The Execution Plan

Not a slogan — a sequence. Six concrete moves, in order, each answering what actually needs to be done. Every step is funded publicly and reported against in the open ledger.

Your Identity Track

From visitor to sovereign — the path every member walks.

Identity & Status

A serious education track on the documented history of racial classification in America — how the ledgers of the state moved a people from "Negro" to "Colored" to "Black" to "African American," and what each relabeling did to rights, records, and standing. The track pairs that history with practice: lineage research through census, Freedmen's Bureau, and church records, and step-by-step guidance for correcting the record — birth, death, and enrollment documents — where the archive got a family wrong.

The full curriculum is routed through the Academy's reading paths: begin with the Erased Towns Sequence, then the Strategist's Path. Enter through the Academy →

Why the ledger matters

Erasure was never only violence — it was bookkeeping. Deeds voided, claims denied, maps redrawn, lakes poured over graves. The Reclamation Ledger answers erasure with its own instruments: documented chapters, an on-chain memorial record, and a rebuild plan with named phases and public milestones. What was taken in the dark is catalogued in the open.

Each chapter below is written respectfully and briefly by design. The full dossiers — oral histories, plat maps, news clippings — live in the Open Archive, stewarded by our Historian in Residence.

“They burned the buildings and thought they had burned the idea. Buildings are cheap. The idea is load-bearing.”— Sefu Maroon, Historian in Residence

Ledger by the numbers

35

Blocks of Greenwood destroyed in under 48 hours in 1921.

11

Lives taken by the 1985 MOVE bombing in Philadelphia — five of them children.

1874

Year the Freedmen's Bank collapsed, erasing the savings of over 60,000 Black depositors.

1

Coups d'état on American soil: Wilmington, 1898. The ledger keeps count.

∞

How long the commons intends to remember.

The Overlooked

Say their names

A living memorial and a working family fund. Remembrance is not passive — it is fuel. Every name below was a whole world: a laugh someone is still waiting to hear, a chair still pulled up to a table. The commons refuses the arithmetic that reduces them to statistics; here they are spoken of in full sentences, and their families are answered in full dollars.

Family Fund

Direct POL donations support families of the overlooked. Current reserve: ◎12,480 POL

The reserve is fed automatically — 20% of all Commons Coin flows route here before anything else is paid. Every disbursement is steward-verified, proposed in the open, voted in the Signal, and published to the ledger.

Report an Overlooked Case

Know a name that belongs on this wall? Add them, with care.

Submissions appear immediately, flagged under steward review until verified against public records.

“Grief that is organized becomes fund. Fund that is organized becomes land. Land that is organized becomes home.”— Imani Castellan, Family Fund Director

How the Family Fund disperses

The fund moves in two channels. The rapid channel answers within seventy-two hours: burial costs, legal retainers, emergency housing for families named on the wall. The endowment channel compounds quietly: scholarships, land down-payments, and small-business grants for the children and grandchildren of the overlooked. Every disbursement is proposed in the open, voted in the Signal, and published to the ledger.

Donations arrive in POL on Polygon — low fees mean a five-dollar gift arrives as five dollars of help, not three dollars and change of friction.

Treasury Commons

Held in common

Every dollar of the commons is allocated openly. This is what collective custody looks like.

$248,000

Multisig-held, community-governed, audited quarterly. Proposals are voted on-chain; execution is public. No dollar in this treasury has an owner — only a purpose, a proposal number, and a paper trail any member can walk end to end.

The figure above is the book value at the last quarterly audit. Land is carried at acquisition cost, never at hope — the commons has learned from history what inflated paper is worth when the music stops.

Multisig custody

Five keys, three required to move a dollar. Keys are held by the Treasury Keeper, two lane leads, one elder seat, and one randomly drawn member each quarter — custody rotates, trust does not concentrate.

Quarterly audit

An independent reviewer walks every transaction against every passed proposal. The report is read aloud, line by line, at the commons assembly — slowly, until everyone understands it.

Proposal pipeline

Any registered member may propose an allocation over $500. Proposals get seven days of discussion, three of voting, and a permanent record in the ledger. Silence is consent; dissent is sacred.

The Blueprint

Three phases to sovereignty

A decade-long arc, broken into deliberate phases. Each phase ends with a community referendum to continue, amend, or stop — because a roadmap the members cannot refuse is just another word for a cage. The timeline below is the current ratified version, amended twice by the Signal and stronger for it.

Referendum gates

No phase begins automatically. At the end of each phase the commons holds a thirty-day referendum: continue, amend, or stop. Sovereignty that cannot be declined is not sovereignty — it is a roadmap with handcuffs. Twice already the membership has amended the blueprint, and both amendments made it better.

What success looks like

Success is not a valuation. It is a Tuesday evening in Phase III: the market hall full, the academy lit, the fund quietly answering a family within the day, and no one anywhere needing to ask permission for any of it.

Community Signal

One member, one voice

Current signal: Where should the next Academy study circle be hosted? Cast your vote below.

How the Signal works

One registered wallet, one vote. No weighting by holdings, no delegation without consent, no quiet quorums. A wallet with a million $COMMONS whispers at exactly the volume of a wallet with one.

Binding, not advisory

Signal results over 60% become binding resolutions at the next assembly. The treasury executes what the Signal decides, publishes the transaction, and reads it aloud at the quarterly audit.

Everything recorded

Polls, tallies, turnout, and the full text of every debate are archived publicly. The commons keeps receipts — especially of its own decisions, most especially of its mistakes.

“Democracy is not the vote. The vote is the last five minutes of democracy. The rest is listening.”— Ayana Freewater, Signal Weaver
Tomorrowland Market

Commerce within the commons

Goods, prints, and offerings from member artisans — priced in $COMMONS, settled instantly on Polygon, and routed through the dignity floor: five percent of every sale to the Family Fund before anyone is paid. Commerce here is not extraction with better branding; it is the commons feeding itself.

Apply to vend

Every vendor in the Tomorrowland Market is a verified Black-owned business and a registered member of the commons. Tell us what you make; the market curator answers within a week.

Market principles

Every seller in the Tomorrowland Market is a registered member; every good is priced in $COMMONS; and five percent of every sale routes automatically to the Family Fund before the seller is paid. The market exists so that wealth circulates inside the commons at least three times before it ever touches an outside bank. Artisans set their own prices — the commons sets only the floor of dignity: no goods made by underpaid hands, ever.

Members OnlyPriced in $COMMONS5% to Family FundDignity Floor
Commons Coin

$COMMONS token allocation

Polygon-native, 21M fixed supply, 1-member-1-vote governance — no inflation switch and no upgrade key. The majority of supply belongs — permanently — to the community, because a coin whose future can be rewritten by a small committee is just a bank with extra steps. We built the alternative instead.

Fixed supply

21M $COMMONS, minted once at genesis on Polygon. No inflation switch exists in the contract — it was never written in, and the contract cannot be upgraded to add one. Scarcity is a promise kept in code.

1 member, 1 vote

Governance ignores balances entirely: one registered member, one vote, whether the wallet holds a million $COMMONS or one. Rewards flow to hours worked, guides taught, cases documented, and land surveyed — belonging is earned in the lanes, never bought.

Locked liquidity

The liquidity allocation is locked for the full ten years of the Blueprint, verifiable on-chain by any member at any hour. The coin serves the plan; the plan does not serve the coin.

$COMMONS is a community utility token for a cooperative demonstration — not an investment product, and nothing on this page is financial advice. The commons sells no promises, only groceries, books, candles, and seats.

The Door Is Open

Build tomorrow with us

Every chapter reclaimed, every shelf sponsored, every name remembered on the wall began with one person signing their name. The commons asks nothing it does not give back: an hour in your lane, a vote in the Signal, a seat at the table that no one else will set for us.
